_demo.purpose: Frontend development and demo fixture. People, companies, facts, dates and chats are fictional; books, films, tools, cities and public places are real.
_demo.persona: Nora Chen, 29, grew up in Austin and lives in San Francisco. A former UI designer and AI product designer, she has worked full time on her own AI product, Murmur, since September 2026.
reusable_rules: Follow the existing profile hierarchy format and dimension ID conventions.
Each fact appears exactly once in the hierarchy, and every source_ids reference must resolve.
Facts under the same attribute add distinct information. All synthetic sources are explicitly marked as fictional.
local_rules: Translated from profile_hierarchy.demo.json fact by fact and chat by chat, localized to the US; fact indices, source ids, dimensions and topics match it.
A second round added life areas a real profile usually has (job hunting, learning, investing, games and anime, devices, friends), on a hand-set list of 16 domains.
Dimension 1 has 12 more hand-written facts and chats, placed in domains by hand.
Chat times keep their wall-clock time in the America/Los_Angeles time zone.
_demo.adaptation: Regenerate the Chinese demo first, then translate it with the same localization.
_demo.review_state: The existing backend initially imports records as pending. Review actions are saved only to a separate demo database.

timeline_variant.purpose: Source times for the opening animation and timeline replay.
rules: The first source of each fact is its first mention; later sources mention it again.
support_count is the fact's number of sources; source_*_mean average the sources' confidence and importance.

facts.value: B was born on June 12, 1997.
B is Nora Chen, a Chinese-American product designer whose friends call her Nora.
B is from Austin, Texas.
B is a woman.
B grew up near South Congress in Austin, Texas.
B studied Industrial Design as an undergraduate at RISD (Rhode Island School of Design) from 2015 to 2019 and graduated with a bachelor's degree in July 2019.
B attended elementary, middle, and high school in Austin, Texas, and first lived away from home for an extended period when she moved to Providence for college in 2015.
B is 163 centimeters tall without shoes, or about 5 feet 4 inches.
B joined Gridline, a fictional collaboration software company in New York, on July 8, 2019, initially as a UI designer, and stopped holding that role after her promotion in March 2021.
B was promoted to senior interaction designer at Gridline in March 2021 and later moved to Glowfield AI in April 2023.
B joined Glowfield AI, a fictional company in San Francisco, as an AI product designer in April 2023 and completed her departure paperwork on September 4, 2026.
B has worked full-time as an independent developer on her own product, Murmur, since leaving Glowfield AI in September 2026.
B moved from New York to San Francisco in April 2023 and has lived in the Inner Sunset ever since; she still lives in San Francisco as of October 2026.
facts.topic: Moving to SF and living arrangements

facts.value: B lived in New York after graduating from college, from July 2019 to April 2023, sharing an apartment in Brooklyn until she moved to San Francisco.
facts.topic: Moving to SF and living arrangements

facts.value: B is an only child and has no siblings.
B adopted a calico cat named Mochi in May 2025; she currently lives with Mochi and handles her daily care alone.
B has a mother who runs a small stationery shop in Austin, Texas.
B has a father who taught high-school physics before retiring.
B has a father who is retired.
B has parents who have always lived near South Congress in Austin, Texas.
B previously dated Ryan Cole, an architect; they began a long-distance relationship between New York and San Francisco after she moved to San Francisco in April 2023, and they broke up in April 2025.
facts.topic: Long-distance dating and rebuilding after a breakup

facts.value: B has not entered a new relationship since breaking up with Ryan Cole in April 2025 and is still single as of October 12, 2026.

facts.value: B has repeatedly been praised by Leo for giving the best demos on the team, despite her lower assessment of her own public speaking skills.
B considers her public speaking skills average and not good enough.
B feels confident in her writing and can read The Mom Test and write interview notes and product descriptions.
B does not know how to create 3D models, materials, or lighting and cannot independently build 3D scenes; her use of Midjourney to generate reference images does not mean she has modeling skills.

B is familiar with rewriting selected text in Notion AI and having multi-turn conversations with ChatGPT, and she can analyze interaction flows in terms of entry points, context, confirmation, and undo.

B is proficient at using Framer to create interface animations and complete task-flow prototypes, including simulated input, conditional branching, navigation, error feedback, expanding and collapsing content, confirmation, and undo; simulated AI output in her prototypes does not mean actual AI functionality has been implemented.

B can independently define interface typography standards and is familiar with type-size hierarchies, line height, and font-weight and baseline adjustments when combining Source Han Sans with Inter; she can align columns of numbers and define tabular-figure rules for monetary amounts, but she cannot design an entire typeface.
B can design notifications for expired login sessions.

B has conducted multiple rounds of user interviews for collaboration software and is skilled at independently developing interview guides, moderating interviews, asking follow-up questions, and synthesizing findings; she has read The Mom Test and knows how to probe specific experiences, reconstruct recent actual behaviors, difficulties, and workarounds, distinguish users' own words from her interpretations, and avoid treating verbal praise or stated willingness to use a product as direct evidence of a user need.

B can define semantic colors, status colors, and corresponding text guidelines, check body-text contrast against WCAG AA, and use text and icons to avoid distinguishing states solely through red and green.
B can review capacity expansion settings interfaces, but this ability does not extend to reviewing deployment plans.

B considers Figma and design systems her strongest skills; she can independently build a component library from scratch and maintain it over time, manage components, variants, variables, and state specifications, and write usage rules, conditions under which components must not be used, and acceptance criteria, and she has experience integrating the system into products, migrating legacy components, mapping design components to code, maintaining deprecation lists, and conducting joint acceptance reviews with engineering.

B understands how to limit the use of account identifiers, log contents, and evaluation samples to their intended purposes, can judge which claims privacy copy can legitimately make, and recognizes that de-identification, logging restrictions, and anonymous evaluation are not equivalent to end-to-end encryption.

B has been learning and practicing prompt design since December 2022 and can break down tasks, supply context, and define output fields and constraints; for journal, to-do, and weekly review tasks, she can refine outputs by distinguishing exact quotes from inferences, preserving the original meaning, separating to-dos from reflections, and prohibiting unsupported additions.

B can break vague negative feedback about an agent into failure categories, design task-specific normal, missing-information, unauthorized-action, and high-risk cases with pass criteria, and separately assess content correctness, permission boundaries, and whether confirmation should be requested first.
facts.topic: Enterprise agent tasks and acceptance criteria

facts.value: B considers herself unfamiliar with underlying model principles and training mechanisms.
B knows that prompt constraints cannot guarantee factual accuracy and that model outputs still need verification.

B is experienced in using fixed inputs to compare how models process spoken Chinese, including before and after a model switch, and can separately assess preservation of meaning, to-do extraction, latency, and cost; she has tested GPT-4o against Claude 3.5 Sonnet and explicitly recognizes that these results cannot establish an overall model ranking or transfer directly to enterprise agent tool-use tasks.

B can independently design evaluation sets for journals, to-dos, and weekly reviews, organizing fixed samples around real problems and covering conversational omissions, ambiguity, negation, self-corrections, missing information, and relative or vague times; she can separately check fact preservation, distorted meaning, omissions, fabricated to-dos, unsupported additions, and emotional wording, and knows that anonymized rewrites must preserve the original samples’ linguistic challenges.

B can write basic Python scripts for organizing files, batch renaming, cleaning CSV data, reading JSON, exporting CSV files, and making batch calls to models or other APIs, including exporting evaluation CSV files, but cannot build a complete service.

B knows basic SQL filtering, grouping, and counting and can query signups, paying users, orders, refunds, and subscription revenue and aggregate them by day, but she is not familiar with complex multi-table joins or performance optimization.

B began learning TypeScript in 2023 and by April 2024 could independently develop and deploy Next.js frontends with help from Cursor and Claude; she retains this ability but rates her TypeScript skills, including type design, and her Next.js skills as average and considers her code inelegant.

B cannot write backend authentication independently and has not mastered token refresh or permission checks; she explicitly distinguishes code generated by Claude from skills she has mastered and relies on Max Zhou for this work on Murmur.

B does not understand Kubernetes or service scaling and cannot independently handle scaling or assess production capacity or deployment options; she relies on Max Zhou for this server-side work on Murmur.
B is familiar with application-layer model integration and can independently handle response structures, output alignment, timeouts, and manual fallback when switching models.

B repeatedly said from 2019 through November 2022 that she could not code and could only design interfaces or create prototypes, not build working applications; she began teaching herself Python with ChatGPT in December 2022 and could write basic scripts by early 2023.
B experienced two App Store rejections while getting the first version of Murmur approved for release.

B is familiar with organizing product retrospectives around problems, solutions, validation, and limitations; she can distinguish signup growth from retention improvements and recognize claims about a feature's effects that are not yet supported by evidence.
B explicitly says she is unfamiliar with paid user acquisition.
B still does not understand company registration or tax filing procedures as of September 2026 and cannot handle these matters independently.
B has completed Apple's privacy review process, including the App Privacy details.
B cannot independently perform complex financial analysis and needs help from others.
B does not know how to lead climb, clip quickdraws, or clean routes, and she explicitly confirmed that she still had not acquired those skills after her May 2026 Joshua Tree trip.

B rated herself at around V2 from September 2023 through January 2024, doing better on routes with large holds but struggling with weight shifts on small footholds; by February–August 2026, she had progressed to around V4 indoors, could complete routes in different styles including vertical walls and slight overhangs, and had learned hip turns, foot swaps, and toe repositioning.

B has long wanted to build products that connect with everyday personal life, help ordinary people express themselves and organize their lives, and make them feel cared for rather than merely improving work efficiency; Murmur puts this direction into practice, and she wants people outside the tech industry with no AI knowledge to be able to use it easily and want to keep recording their lives.
B remains motivated by a desire to move away from the impersonal feel of business software and hopes Murmur will make people want to record their lives.

B wants new users of enterprise collaboration software to be able to create projects and invite coworkers independently without reading documentation or receiving training, lowering the barrier to their first collaboration.

B wants Murmur's diary entries and weekly reviews to stay faithful to users' own expression, tone, and actual experiences, without replacing their voices with polished prose, inventing emotions, promises, or personal growth, or automatically turning negative expressions into motivational messages or narratives of striving for success.
B wants Murmur to help users reread and connect the experiences they have recorded and understand themselves, rather than merely accumulate and store entries.

B wants AI to do the work involved in recording, organizing, and reviewing, reducing users' need to piece together context, confirm things repeatedly, answer follow-up questions, and handle failures; she wants to evaluate the experience by task completion and recovery from failures rather than by increasing conversation turns or time spent in the app, so users can finish recording and return to their lives.

B wants Murmur to remain warm and supportive without driving usage or product growth through guilt over missed entries, pressure to maintain streaks, performance-review-style weekly reports, or scores for users' lives.

B wants users to understand and take over AI actions, controlling results through clear task statuses, confirmation of key actions, before-and-after comparisons of organized content, editing, and undo, rather than simply eliminating chat entry points.
B wants users to be able to retrieve their diaries at any time, even after they stop using Murmur, so restrictions on their records do not prevent them from leaving.

B wants Murmur to let people who want to record their lives but cannot bring themselves to write simply speak for a moment and receive usable, editable diary entries and to-dos, without having to organize their thoughts in advance, learn complicated operations or prompts, master conversational techniques, keep chatting, or repeatedly rework the output.
B wants to standardize components and design rules and drive actual adoption of the design system, reducing repetitive drawing so she can spend design time researching and mapping user flows.

B wants AI products to understand user intent and complete tasks directly, producing usable, editable results while reducing the need to learn prompting or repeatedly move context between tools, rather than substituting a chat window or multiple conversational turns for end-to-end task completion.
facts.topic: Enterprise agent tasks and acceptance criteria

facts.value: B wants enterprise agents to reduce workloads while preserving users’ decision-making authority, making task progress visible, allowing confirmation of critical and high-risk actions, supporting stopping or undoing execution, and enabling recovery and remediation after failures.
facts.topic: Enterprise agent tasks and acceptance criteria

facts.value: B wants to improve asynchronous collaboration on Murmur so Max Zhou can understand changes and how to verify that they meet requirements from documentation alone.

B wants to independently deliver products from implementing designs and modifying interactions through deploying the frontend so she can iterate on Murmur herself and reduce her dependence on other people's help and development schedules, rather than become a full-stack engineer.
B wants Murmur to retain journal export functionality while supporting multi-device sync, protecting users' ability to retrieve their entries over the long term.
B wants to stay in San Francisco and build Murmur into a long-term business; she does not currently want to return to Austin, Texas, to pursue her career.
B wants to keep developing and running Murmur for many years without relying on chronic late nights or short-term overexertion.

B wants Murmur to remain affordable for ordinary users over the long term and clearly display total prices, price changes, and renewal information; she does not want to generate revenue or harm the user experience by creating anxiety, exploiting users' failure to notice prices, obscuring renewals, or pursuing aggressive monetization.

B wants Murmur to build a base of retained users who keep journaling over the long term through recommendations driven by genuine usefulness, everyday community conversations, and ongoing contact, rather than depending on a one-time platform feature, conference exposure, virality, or maintaining an influencer persona by chasing trends every day; she also does not want to force users to share in exchange for feature rewards or access to normal functionality.

B wants ongoing contact with real Murmur users, including users abroad, to gather feedback about specific use cases, obstacles, and reasons for stopping use after paying, so she can validate their willingness to keep journaling over the long term and the product's actual usefulness rather than relying only on signups, follows, saves, rankings, short-term exposure, or community size.
B wants Murmur's recurring income to cover her living expenses and support long-term independent product development so she no longer needs to subsidize it with a salary or draw down her savings.

B wants Murmur to generate stable, ongoing customer payments and subscription revenue that cover operating costs such as models, servers, and maintenance and support long-term operations; she values a stable business more than a short-term surge in users and does not want to depend on launch buzz or the next funding round.

B wants investment to give her a stable runway for developing and refining Murmur and support its long-term operation while she retains control over product direction, without turning it into a sales tool for enterprise customers to secure funding.

B wants to use a unified document to record review decisions, project status, and acceptance criteria so remote teammates who were absent can stay informed, reducing reliance on individual memory, repeated discussions, and rework rather than increasing the number of documents.
B hopes to broaden her career options by taking her own product all the way through launch, rather than merely changing her professional title to engineer.

B wants to build products independently over the long term, choosing which problems to solve, setting product direction, and taking responsibility for the outcomes, rather than simply having fewer meetings.

B wants to reserve half a day each week for photography, reading, or watching films without monetizing those activities or treating them as work output; as of September 2026, she was still working toward that arrangement.

B wants to control when she works and stops working, keep most Murmur work in daytime hours, and build a lifestyle she can sustain for years rather than relying on a day job plus nighttime work, continually staying up late, or sacrificing sleep for releases.
B wants to maintain a long-term budget for basic health and accident insurance and will not cut that coverage even if she works independently, develops products on her own, or reduces other expenses.
B does not want to use her parents' money to fund her startup; she wants to keep startup funding separate from their retirement savings and does not consider her parents a source of financing.
B wants to keep her personal emergency fund separate from her product funds rather than invest all of it in Murmur, so she retains a fallback.
B wants to maintain a quiet home where she can live alone and set her own schedule without coordinating with roommates; even when considering spending cuts, she prioritizes continuing to live alone.

facts.value: B wants to stay in San Francisco long-term to build her own work and life while continuing to develop AI products and Murmur; her choice of city reflects her own goals, and she does not want to move back to New York or Austin because others pressure her to.

facts.value: B wants Mom to do less heavy lifting and spend fewer evenings staffing the shop over the long term, so she no longer carries full boxes of paper alone or stays at the shop until 9 p.m. every day, genuinely easing her workload.

B wants Murmur to generate steady, ongoing income before telling her parents that she has left her job to work on the product full-time, using actual income rather than funding that has not arrived to explain how she will support herself.

facts.value: B wants to return to Austin to visit her parents at least twice a year, rather than spending time with them only during Lunar New Year.

facts.value: B wants to stay connected with Lily Shaw outside work and keep sharing their lives, rather than only discussing Murmur updates and forwarding links.

facts.value: B wants to rebuild the stamina she has lost from sedentary work, have energy left after climbing, and maintain the fitness she needs for travel and climbing over the long term rather than rush to climb higher grades.

B wants to gradually learn to assess the challenges of outdoor routes and the limits of her own abilities so she can explain her assessment clearly to an instructor and discuss route choices; she is in no hurry to climb independently without an instructor.

B wants to maintain her climbing ability and physical fitness over the long term so she can still climb in Joshua Tree ten years from now, prioritizing wrist protection over simply pursuing higher grades now.

facts.value: B wants to keep making time for climbing and the outdoors over the long term, without letting Murmur development take over her life or treating exercise as a reward she can have only after all her work is done.
B wants to turn out the lights and go to sleep before midnight so she has more energy during the day; as of October 2026, she had not managed to do this consistently.
B wants steady energy throughout the day without increasing her coffee intake to compensate for insufficient sleep or get through product launches, but she does not plan to give up coffee.

B wants to eat three meals at regular times without sacrificing her stomach health even during product launches, so she can eat comfortably and experience less discomfort from spicy food rather than give it up entirely.

B hopes to build a family photo archive over ten years, documenting her parents' everyday lives, changes in the South Congress neighborhood where she grew up, and everyday objects in Mom's stationery shop, accompanied by her parents' words and related stories for future reflection rather than keeping only travel photos; the archive is not yet complete.

B hopes to maintain a public record of her product experience over the long term, including charging for the first time and having an app submission rejected, to give other developers and designers submitting their first apps useful guidance and help them avoid pitfalls, rather than merely posting price-increase notices.
B hopes her posts on X will help people understand that AI products should focus on real interaction flows rather than simply being chat boxes.
B has access to a paid Figma seat and a paid Framer account provided by Gridline, a fictional collaboration software company, without having to pay for them herself.
B can also work on Murmur during the day after leaving her job in September 2026 and can collaborate remotely with Max Zhou.

B prefers a product's first screen and overview page to explain directly what it is for and what it helps users accomplish.
B is comfortable with gentle prompts in Murmur, but she dislikes AI using anthropomorphic, intimate language such as "I missed you" to drive engagement; she would rather it remain a quiet tool.

B prefers choosing AI interaction patterns based on specific tasks and outcomes, with direct controls, optional actions, and execution status; she accepts chat when it suits the task but opposes using a single, always-present chat box to handle every operation or serve as the only entry point merely to create an AI feel or reuse the same interface.

B does not object to brands using purple, but she has long disliked purple gradients, purple orbs, lighting effects, glowing backgrounds, or star decorations applied solely to create an AI or tech aesthetic; she cares more about a clear purpose, clear buttons, and a clear information hierarchy.
B prefers clear, restrained prompts from enterprise AI agents and dislikes cutesy or wheedling action copy.

B likes Murmur to retain original transcripts so users can easily compare them alongside edited versions, and she wants weekly recaps to keep readily accessible links to original entries and audio playback rather than burying them.

B prefers selecting source text to act on it directly, seeing results beside the original, and being able to edit journal wording or AI report titles directly; she dislikes having to switch to a chat box and send instructions even for minor edits.

B habitually starts by building a clickable prototype of a small, key flow in Framer, walks through it herself, and then has coworkers, engineers, or people unfamiliar with the proposal try it to validate waiting states, errors, and return paths before refining details, expanding pages, or moving into code, rather than waiting until a complete high-fidelity design is ready to show.
B prefers brief, subtle, and clear state transitions or save feedback; she dislikes endlessly spinning orbs during waits or fireworks every time she saves.
B prefers Murmur to sync quietly while keeping its status available to check; she dislikes a notification popping up after every successful sync.
B prefers Murmur's weekly recaps to show what actually happened; she dislikes scoring her life or adding rankings and competitive encouragement such as how many people she has outperformed.
B likes simple icons with consistent stroke widths, and she would rather keep text labels for tool icons whose meanings are unclear or easily misunderstood, such as archive icons.
B prefers displays of actual processing stages; she dislikes fake progress bars and descriptions of ordinary retrieval as "thinking deeply."
B prefers reviewing failure and exit paths before the success flow when evaluating an agent or multistep process; she dislikes demos that show only successful scenarios.
B prefers users to select and confirm AI-extracted task suggestions first, rather than automatically turning passing thoughts, wishes, or future intentions into committed tasks.
B prefers batch actions to be available directly after selecting content in a table; she dislikes turning batch processing into a conversation.
B prefers clicking to confirm rather than typing confirmation text.
B prefers tabular numerals in usage tables and prices.
B prefers Murmur users to go straight to the main interface, with microphone permissions explained when they actually tap to record; she dislikes multipage introductions on first launch.

B prefers AI to preserve users' original words, tone, and genuine feelings, including negative feelings; she dislikes formulaic reassurance, forced praise, emotional coaching, unsolicited judgments that someone is lonely, affectionate pet names, or turning ordinary entries and sadness into lessons about personal growth.
B prefers Murmur to have a quiet interface without excessive decoration, with an off-white background, clear dark text, and clean backgrounds for images shared from the app.
B prefers PingFang or Source Han Sans for Chinese body text, prioritizes comfortable reading of long passages, and dislikes handwritten or attention-grabbing decorative fonts.
B prefers dark gray backgrounds and off-white text; she dislikes the stark contrast of pure black and pure white, especially when reading long passages at night.
B likes soft, warm-toned gradients on covers, including Murmur's weekly recap covers, but she does not want gradients behind body text.
B prefers statuses to be conveyed through color paired with text; she dislikes relying solely on red and green dots to distinguish success from failure or using error red as a decorative color.

B consistently uses The Mom Test-style questions, first letting users describe their most recent actual use experience in their own order, including the context, process, existing approach, interruption points, and workarounds, and showing a proposed solution only after listening; she does not substitute feature votes, polite praise, or hypothetical willingness to use something for behavioral evidence.
B likes whitespace on home screens and dislikes task lists filled with large cards, but she wants work tables used for looking up data to stay compact and information-dense.
B dislikes secondary text that is too faint to read and wants important explanations and subscription renewal details to use clearly readable font sizes and colors.
B prefers a clear hierarchy built with a small set of font sizes, font weights, and whitespace; she dislikes using seven or eight font sizes on one screen.
B prefers restrained, slightly rounded corners and is fine with pill-shaped tags, but she dislikes screens full of pill-shaped elements or pill-shaped panels.

B prefers restrained, neutral, low-saturation base colors, status colors used as needed, and a single accent color to highlight primary actions; she dislikes multiple bright colors competing for attention.
B habitually checks existing components before building a page and prioritizes reuse without forcing a fit; she does not want to redraw or maintain duplicate versions of the same kinds of buttons.
B prefers deriving a sufficient component library from recurring real needs rather than building unused components in advance for the sake of completeness.
B habitually groups button states such as default, hover, disabled, and loading into the same variant set in Figma rather than placing them separately.
B likes Inter for English-language interfaces.
B prefers being able to open Murmur and start speaking with one tap, without choosing a category or entering a title first; she is fine with adding a mood category after recording.
B habitually includes loading, empty, error, and retry states before handing off designs, rather than providing only ideal success screens.
B prefers breakdowns of earlier drafts, failed approaches, and hands-on techniques at design conferences, rather than slides full of trend buzzwords.

B dislikes vague feedback such as “make it more polished,” “give it more feeling,” or unsupported claims that something “feels like AI”; she prefers feedback identifying the specific page, affected users, blocked step, and problem, and habitually asks for the evidence behind it.
B prefers Biscuit to share real situations in which people use Murmur, verbatim user comments, and points where users get stuck, finding these more useful than general praise.

B has consistently named Figma files after lines of poetry since college, for both work and personal projects; she adds project names, business-area indexes, page directories, or notes to clarify functionality and versions, does not want to remove the poetry, and dislikes names like “final final version.”

B usually explains the user task, outcome, and complete workflow before discussing static mockups, typography, and colors; when reviewing a homepage, she starts with information hierarchy and dislikes beginning with comparisons of how “premium” it looks.
B habitually adds realistically long names, long sentences, and empty-data states to designs early, rather than making pages look better using only short text or placeholder content.

B habitually preserves interviewees’ exact words and records her interpretations separately; she does not present guesses as shared conclusions or directly rewrite user problems as requests for a particular solution.

B prefers error messages that explain which step failed, why, and what to do next rather than a generic "Something went wrong"; when Murmur fails to sync, she wants it to state clearly that the entry is saved on the device, syncing failed, and she can retry.

B wants Murmur to show an organized journal entry and tasks directly after users finish speaking, with journal entries, tasks, or weekly recap results displayed right on the home screen and follow-up questions asked only as needed; she dislikes adding a general-purpose chat home screen or an all-purpose entry point and wants users to return to their lives after recording.
B prefers naming component and page colors by purpose, using semantic names such as “surface” while retaining the underlying color scales, rather than relying only on hues or numbered shades.

B prefers the main interface to emphasize primary actions, with advanced options such as model selection and temperature collapsed or tucked into settings; she dislikes a home screen full of parameters.
B prefers AI products that demonstrate specific problems and before-and-after differences, and is less inclined to click promotions for all-purpose assistants emphasizing “the most powerful model.”

facts.value: B likes Claude’s Chinese phrasing and often uses it to tighten Murmur’s copy and release notes, but never adopts its output unchanged; she personally removes clichés, inspirational platitudes, and sentimental endings, preferring restrained, short sentences.

B prefers agents to show their proposed actions and obtain human confirmation before sending emails, bulk-deleting records, or modifying calendars, and dislikes agents performing these actions on their own.

B does not send verbatim investment negotiations or actual valuations directly to Claude; she habitually replaces identities, numbers, and details locally first.

B likes using ChatGPT to brainstorm names, copy, and ideas, usually asking for three distinct directions before exploring each through follow-up questions; she then writes or rewrites the material herself rather than directly using the first draft or copying entire passages.

B habitually asks Claude to find flaws, check assumptions, and look for counterexamples before discussing implementation when she discusses a product or shares a proposed approach with it; she dislikes receiving only affirmation.
B habitually revisits the exact words and checks the source text when reviewing AI abstracts, summaries, or organized Murmur entries, rather than simply accepting their conclusions.
B opposes AI inventing reminders and deadlines.

B checks the purpose of every sentence when writing or revising Murmur’s prompts, retaining only the task, necessary constraints, and clear explanations of output fields; she removes exaggerated role descriptions, useless content, and duplicate requirements, states each requirement only once, and dislikes lengthy all-purpose prompts.

B habitually starts agent demos by asking what happens when execution fails, permissions are missing, or the agent gets stuck; she prefers products that acknowledge uncertainty, explain fallback options, and support human takeover.
facts.topic: Enterprise agent tasks and acceptance criteria

facts.value: B prefers choosing models by task complexity: she starts with inexpensive, sufficiently capable, fast models for simple to-dos and routine organization, but considers journal context and weekly reviews separately and is willing to wait for deeper reasoning; she dislikes using the most expensive model for everything or downgrading every task indiscriminately.

B consistently uses fixed inputs and evaluation sets when modifying Murmur’s prompts, trying new AI products, or comparing candidate models, rather than relying only on polished official examples; she includes spoken self-corrections, sentence fragments, vague times, and actions the speaker has not committed to, and separately checks for missed to-dos, distorted meaning, and fabricated tasks.

B prefers hiding model names and comparing anonymous outputs side by side using the same batch of inputs, judging output quality first, then speed, cost, and model names, rather than choosing by brand or leaderboard rankings.

B likes using Midjourney to explore color palettes, lighting, mood, and composition, but does not copy buttons, text, or entire page designs from its results or directly use generated images as final icons.

B typically changes only one feature or fixes one issue at a time when developing Murmur with Cursor or Claude, reviews diffs in small chunks, and runs the code herself to verify it before continuing; she dislikes whole-page or whole-file rewrites and generating a complete implementation in one go.
B prefers to keep both versions and let users choose when Murmur encounters content conflicts across devices, rather than silently overwrite either version.
B typically provides screenshots, reproduction steps, and her own assessment or hypothesis before discussing Murmur issues with Max Zhou, and she wants him to point out mistakes directly.
B prefers learning Python by watching lessons while doing practical tasks such as organizing files and renaming screenshots, rather than repeatedly solving coding problems or doing exercises alone.
B prefers learning TypeScript through specific webpage requirements and looking up relevant information as needed, rather than watching an entire course first.

B usually starts troubleshooting Murmur issues by reviewing the steps taken and the errors; only when the original text is truly necessary does she ask users to voluntarily excerpt the relevant passages, redact private information, and separately confirm their consent.
B typically writes clear reproduction steps and expected results for Murmur feedback before adding it to Linear, rather than treating chat screenshots as tasks.
B dislikes offering membership rewards in exchange for reposts and prefers voluntary recommendations based on genuine experience with the product.

B organizes product and launch retrospectives around user friction points, changes, and results rather than a chronological development log; she also starts her Product Hunt retrospective with user friction points and puts the ranking in the summary.

B prefers to demonstrate products through real interfaces and actual use, uses only screenshots of currently available features in app store images, and presents the flow in the order of speaking, journaling, and to-dos; she dislikes concept images passed off as actual products, concept animations, oversized chat boxes, and decorative AI branding, prefers the Product Hunt cover to emphasize the journal entry itself, and also dislikes using a valuation as a demo cover.
B cares more about whether users are still using the product two weeks later and does not treat its Product Hunt ranking as a measure of its value.
B prefers straightforward monthly prices, annual prices, and renewal terms, dislikes reframing prices as just a few cents a day, and objects to fake discount countdowns.

B prefers investors who have actually used Murmur and can discuss specific experiences with it, and she dislikes investors who immediately push paid user acquisition or urge her to pivot to enterprise projects.
B does not want to make investment negotiations or valuations public and does not want Lily Shaw to relay the figures being discussed.

B consistently kept business materials separate from negotiation materials containing valuations and her bottom line on concessions during the October 2026 funding discussions, sending the latter only to investors in separate messages.
B asks for key investment terms in writing first, reads them one by one before responding, and dislikes agreeing on the spot over the phone.
B preferred letting users experience Murmur fully during its free phase from March through August 2024 and disliked showing payment prompts too early.
B has preferred subscription pricing for Murmur since February 2025 and still held that preference in November of the same year.
B preferred a clear, single payment to unlock features when Murmur began charging in September 2024 and disliked charging separately for small features.
B rewrites demo samples as fictional text and replaces names, companies, and specific locations rather than merely removing names.

B first gives a small group of existing users access to new Murmur versions rather than releasing them to everyone at once, and she continued this practice after leaving her job to work on Murmur full-time.
B prefers written feedback from the community and users and also accepts short screen recordings, but she dislikes unexpected calls or minute-long voice memos.

B does not want to disclose Murmur's actual revenue publicly and shares it only with people close to her or a limited circle of acquaintances; she prefers discussing methods and lessons learned in public and also does not want to discuss her savings in a public retrospective about leaving her job.
B reviews Murmur's bills every Sunday evening and uses the number of valid journal entries to track the cost per valid entry; she dislikes lowering bills by cutting content that should be recorded.
B records and labels sign-up, trial, and paying-user counts separately in retrospectives rather than broadly describing sign-ups as users served.

B prefers small-screen phones that are comfortable to hold, easy to operate securely with one hand, and fit in her pocket; she is unwilling to sacrifice hand comfort for a larger display and does not seek a bigger screen for watching videos.

B is interested in trying the Switch 2 but prefers to wait until there is an exclusive game she really wants to play before considering buying one or upgrading, rather than buying it simply because it is new.

B was still using the MacBook Air M1 she bought in 2021 as her primary personal computer as of September 2026, running Cursor and her local Murmur development environment on it; she switched to a Mac mini for her primary day-to-day work in October 2026.

B stores her film scans in her subscribed 2 TB iCloud storage plan.
B usually reads books on her Kindle and looks up unfamiliar words by pressing and holding them; she is not used to switching between a reading app and a dictionary on her phone.
B checks privacy settings first when setting up a new phone, tablet, or computer, turning off tracking, personalized ads, and optional usage data sharing wherever possible before installing apps.
